A.explanation: An electron antineutrino is emitted in neutron beta-minus decay to conserve lepton number and energy-momentum.

B.explanation: A down quark in the neutron changes into an up quark to turn the neutron into a proton.

C.explanation: No positron is emitted; neutron decay is beta-minus decay which emits an electron, not its antiparticle the positron.

D.explanation: Up quarks are involved because the neutron contains up quarks and a new up quark is formed in the proton.

hints: Recall the full beta-minus equation for a free neutron: neutron becomes proton plus electron plus antineutrino.
Think at quark level: a neutron is $udd$ and a proton is $uud$, so one quark flavour must change.
Check charge and lepton number: the emitted lepton must be negative to balance $0$ to $+1$, so decide electron versus positron.
walkthrough: Write the nucleon change: $n$ to $p$. The proton has one more positive charge, so a negatively charged lepton must be emitted.
The full beta-minus decay is $n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$, so an electron and an electron antineutrino are both involved.
At quark level, $udd$ becomes $uud$, which means a down quark changes to an up quark, so both down and up quarks are involved.
A positron $e^+$ appears only in beta-plus decay when a proton becomes a neutron, not here.
Therefore the positron is the particle not involved. This is option C.
